*This page is the course's learning library: a short, curated set of
resources for going further, organized by the part of the course they
extend. It is not the evidence ledger. That lives in
`sources/source-map.md` and `sources/claims.csv`, which answer a
different question ("what supports this factual statement?") and list
every cited source with its exact locator. Some papers appear in both
places, because a primary source can also be good reading;
where that is so, the entry says why it is recommended as reading.*

*Every link on this page was opened on 2026-09-15. Durations are given
only where the resource's own page states them. Vendor documentation
changes without notice: for those entries, treat the description as of
the access date, and reread the current page rather than memorizing
its syntax.*

## Foundations: neural networks and learning

### 3Blue1Brown, *Neural Networks* (chapters 1–5)

- **Creator:** Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown)
- **Format:** video series with written adaptations; five chapters from
  2017 ("But what is a Neural Network?", "Gradient descent, how neural
  networks learn", "Analyzing our neural network", "What is
  backpropagation really doing?", "Backpropagation calculus")
- **Level:** introductory, strongly visual; no code
- **Useful for:** seeing the multi-layer case of everything the
  neural-networks lesson works by hand on one unit: units, layers,
  gradient descent, and backpropagation, animated on a real
  digit-recognition network
- **Limitation:** the examples are image classification, not language;
  the site's own chapter numbering restarts for its later
  transformer lessons, so "chapter 5" is ambiguous across the two series
- **Link:** <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/neural-networks>
  (chapter 1; each lesson links to the next)

### Michael Nielsen, *Neural Networks and Deep Learning*

- **Creator:** Michael Nielsen
- **Format:** free online book, six chapters (Determination Press,
  2015; last updated December 2019)
- **Level:** introductory to intermediate; assumes comfort with algebra
  and some calculus, and reads code
- **Useful for:** a patient, complete derivation of backpropagation
  (chapter 2) and a visual argument for why networks can represent
  arbitrary functions (chapter 4); a strong free text for readers who
  want the mathematics of the neural-networks lesson in full
- **Limitation:** the code is written in Python 2.7, which is no longer
  supported, and the book predates transformers entirely
- **Link:** <http://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/>

### Andrej Karpathy, *Neural Networks: Zero to Hero*

- **Creator:** Andrej Karpathy
- **Format:** eight video lectures, building everything from scratch in
  code; the syllabus page states each lecture's length (the first, on
  backpropagation, is 2h25m; the GPT lecture is 1h56m; the tokenizer
  lecture is 2h13m)
- **Level:** intermediate; requires solid Python and introductory
  calculus, and is meant to be followed at a keyboard
- **Useful for:** turning the course's concepts into working code: a
  hand-written backpropagation engine, a character-level language
  model, a small GPT, and a byte pair encoding tokenizer
- **Limitation:** long and hands-on; the page describes the course as
  ongoing, so its scope may change
- **Link:** <https://karpathy.ai/zero-to-hero.html>

## Transformers and language models

### 3Blue1Brown, *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs* and *Attention in transformers, step-by-step*

- **Creator:** Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown); text adaptations by
  Justin Sun
- **Format:** two video lessons with written versions (Deep Learning
  chapters 5 and 6, April 2024)
- **Level:** introductory, strongly visual
- **Useful for:** the animated counterparts of the course's softmax,
  temperature, and attention pages: why softmax needs a normalizing
  sum, how temperature reshapes a distribution, and how query, key, and
  value vectors combine
- **Limitation:** leans on the "what is this token looking for" reading
  of attention more freely than this course does, and does not cover
  the multinomial-logit bridge or the training objective
- **Links:** <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt>,
  <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/attention>

### Jay Alammar, *The Illustrated Transformer*

- **Creator:** Jay Alammar
- **Format:** illustrated blog post (June 2018; positional-encoding
  section updated July 2020), with a companion post *The Illustrated
  GPT-2* (August 2019) on the decoder-only case
- **Level:** introductory to intermediate; light mathematics
- **Useful for:** a diagram-by-diagram walk through the original
  encoder–decoder Transformer, including multi-head attention and the
  residual and normalization structure the attention deep dive
  describes in words
- **Limitation:** describes the 2017 translation model, not a modern
  decoder-only language model; the GPT-2 post's author lists his own
  simplifications (words and tokens used interchangeably, inference
  shown rather than training)
- **Links:** <https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/>,
  <https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-gpt2/>

### Andrej Karpathy, *Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT*

- **Creator:** Andrej Karpathy
- **Format:** single long video (YouTube, published February 2025)
- **Level:** introductory, plain language, no equations
- **Useful for:** the whole pipeline in one sitting, from tokenization
  through pretraining, post-training, and inference, with real
  tokenizers and real generation loops on screen; the narrative anchor
  for this course's short story
- **Limitation:** no mathematics, and long enough to watch in segments
- **Link:** <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI>

### Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*

- **Creator:** Ashish Vaswani and colleagues (Google Brain, Google
  Research, University of Toronto)
- **Format:** paper, arXiv:1706.03762 (v7, 2023-08-02); Sections 3 and 4
  are the parts the course uses
- **Level:** technical
- **Useful for:** the primary source and, unusually for a primary
  source, still a clear, short statement of the architecture: the
  attention equations, the block structure, and Table 1's comparison of
  recurrent and self-attention layers. Recommended as reading, not only
  as evidence, because the course's why-transformers and attention pages
  are built directly on it
- **Limitation:** a machine-translation encoder–decoder model; the
  decoder-only form used by language models gets one paragraph
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

### Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Jauvin, *A Neural Probabilistic Language Model*

- **Creator:** Yoshua Bengio, Réjean Ducharme, Pascal Vincent, Christian
  Jauvin
- **Format:** paper, Journal of Machine Learning Research 3 (2003),
  1137–1155; Sections 1 and 2 carry the ideas
- **Level:** technical, but the first two sections are readable without
  the rest
- **Useful for:** a clear early statement of two ideas the course
  depends on, a learned vector per vocabulary entry and next-token
  maximum likelihood, in a setting simple enough to see them without a
  transformer around them
- **Limitation:** the network is not a transformer and the vocabulary is
  words, not subword tokens
- **Link:** <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf>

### Hugging Face, *LLM Course*

- **Creator:** Hugging Face
- **Format:** free web course, twelve chapters, with runnable code using
  the Hugging Face libraries; originally an NLP course, since extended
  to large language models, fine-tuning, and reasoning models
- **Level:** intermediate; the course states that it requires good
  Python and is best taken after an introductory deep-learning course
- **Useful for:** working with real tokenizers, pretrained models, and
  fine-tuning code after the conceptual lessons here
- **Limitation:** tied to one library ecosystem, and revised
  continuously, so chapter contents move
- **Link:** <https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course/chapter1/1>

## Training and post-training

### Ouyang et al., *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback*

- **Creator:** Long Ouyang and colleagues (OpenAI)
- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2203.02155 (v1, 2022-03-04); the abstract and
  Section 3 describe the recipe
- **Level:** technical
- **Useful for:** the primary description of the supervised, then
  reward-model, then reinforcement-learning recipe; the paper reports
  that, in its evaluations, outputs from a much smaller post-trained
  model were preferred to outputs from the much larger pretrained GPT-3
  model. Recommended as reading because Section 3 is a concrete,
  well-labeled account of what each stage does
- **Limitation:** one provider's 2022 recipe; current recipes vary, and
  the paper's "RLHF" is one route, not post-training as a whole
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155>

### Rafailov et al., *Direct Preference Optimization*

- **Creator:** Rafael Rafailov and colleagues (Stanford)
- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2305.18290 (v3, 2024-07-29); the introduction
  carries the idea, the body the derivation
- **Level:** technical; the derivation needs some comfort with
  optimization
- **Useful for:** seeing why the separate reward model can be folded
  into a direct loss on preference pairs; a clear demonstration that
  preference-based post-training can be implemented without the classic
  separate reward-model and online reinforcement-learning pipeline
- **Limitation:** its comparison results are for the tasks and scales
  tested; it is not a verdict that one route has replaced the other
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290>

### DeepSeek-AI, *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning*

- **Creator:** DeepSeek-AI
- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2501.12948 (v2, 2026-01-04); the abstract and
  introduction distinguish R1-Zero from R1
- **Level:** technical
- **Useful for:** a detailed public account of reinforcement
  learning against rule-based, checkable rewards producing long
  reasoning traces, and of why the pure-RL model and the released
  multi-stage model are different objects
- **Limitation:** one lab's recipe; the traces it shows are outputs, not
  transcripts of internal computation, and other providers publish
  less
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948>

## Agents and practical use

### Anthropic, *Building effective agents*

- **Creator:** Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang (Anthropic)
- **Format:** engineering article, published 2024-12-19, accessed
  2026-09-15
- **Level:** practitioner
- **Useful for:** the workflow-versus-agent vocabulary this course uses,
  a short catalogue of composable patterns, and a clear case for the
  simplest system that works
- **Limitation:** one provider's guidance for developers; the page now
  carries its own note that much of the tooling landscape it describes
  has changed since December 2024 [S-73]
- **Link:** <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents>

### Anthropic, *Effective context engineering for AI agents*

- **Creator:** Anthropic Applied AI team
- **Format:** engineering article, published 2025-09-29, accessed
  2026-09-15
- **Level:** practitioner
- **Useful for:** the working definition of context as a finite resource
  and the named practices (just-in-time loading, progressive
  disclosure, compaction, structured notes) that the practical guide
  uses
- **Limitation:** one provider's guidance about its own models, not a
  peer-reviewed result; the course pairs it with the empirical study
  cited in the tokens-and-context deep dive
- **Link:** <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents>

### Lilian Weng, *LLM Powered Autonomous Agents*

- **Creator:** Lilian Weng
- **Format:** long blog post, June 2023
- **Level:** intermediate; survey style, with references
- **Useful for:** an independent, vendor-neutral survey of the agent
  pattern (planning, memory, tool use) with case studies and a candid
  section on challenges; a useful counterweight to reading only
  provider guidance
- **Limitation:** written in 2023, before most current agent tooling,
  and it uses "memory" more loosely than this course, which separates
  parameters, context, and external state
- **Link:** <https://lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/>

### Hugging Face, *AI Agents Course*

- **Creator:** Hugging Face
- **Format:** free web course, units 0–4 plus bonus units, with code in
  several agent frameworks (smolagents, LlamaIndex, LangGraph); the
  page estimates three to four hours of work per week
- **Level:** intermediate; assumes basic Python and basic familiarity
  with language models
- **Useful for:** building the tool-call loop from this course's agents
  lesson yourself, in more than one framework
- **Limitation:** framework-specific code that will date; the page
  describes itself as a living project
- **Link:** <https://huggingface.co/learn/agents-course/unit0/introduction>

### Current provider prompting guidance (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google)

- **Creator:** Anthropic; OpenAI; Google
- **Format:** three living documentation pages, all accessed 2026-09-15;
  only Google's shows a last-updated date
- **Level:** practitioner
- **Useful for:** the point made in the practical guide's section on
  prompting: read the guidance for the model you are using, on the day
  you use it, and notice that the three providers give different
  defaults on the same questions
- **Limitation:** each is tied to its provider's current models and is
  revised without notice; do not memorize their syntax
- **Links:**
  <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices>,
  <https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering>,
  <https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/prompting-strategies>

### Anthropic, Claude Code documentation (best practices, skills, permissions)

- **Creator:** Anthropic
- **Format:** living documentation pages, accessed 2026-09-15
- **Level:** practitioner
- **Useful for:** the concrete product behind the coding-agent examples
  in the agents lesson and the practical guide: verification as
  evidence, planning before implementing, skills as context, and
  software-enforced permissions
- **Limitation:** product-specific; the habits transfer, the commands
  and modes do not, and the pages state that their patterns are not
  fixed
- **Links:** <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices>,
  <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills>,
  <https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions>

## Deeper courses and reference

### Stanford CS224N, *Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning*

- **Creator:** Stanford University (Winter 2026 offering taught by Diyi
  Yang and Yejin Choi)
- **Format:** university lecture course; slides and notes are public,
  and the course page links a complete public lecture-video playlist
  from 2024, while the current term's videos are for enrolled students
- **Level:** advanced undergraduate or graduate; assumes calculus,
  linear algebra, probability, and Python
- **Useful for:** the full academic treatment behind this course's
  conceptual path, from word vectors and recurrent networks to
  transformers, pretraining, and post-training, with problem sets
- **Limitation:** substantial time commitment; the public videos lag the
  current syllabus by a year or more
- **Link:** <https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/>
